title: The Things We Would Do Differently
content:
Mara had always believed that adulthood would become easier with time. When she was younger, she had imagined that people eventually reached a point when decisions stopped feeling complicated, bills became nothing more than numbers on a screen, and mornings no longer began with the uneasy sensation that something important had been forgotten. At thirty-two, however, she had discovered that adulthood was less about finding certainty and more about learning how to live comfortably with uncertainty.

She was sitting at the small kitchen table on a rainy Tuesday evening, staring at a cup of coffee that had long since gone cold. Her laptop remained open beside her, displaying an unfinished report she had promised to send before the end of the day. The apartment was unusually quiet. Outside, rain tapped steadily against the windows, and the occasional headlights of passing cars briefly illuminated the ceiling.

Her phone vibrated.

It was a message from her younger sister, Clara.

— Are you awake?

Mara smiled despite herself.

— Unfortunately.

The reply came almost immediately.

— Can I call you?

A few seconds later, her phone rang.

— You sound terrible — Clara said as soon as Mara answered.

— Thank you. That's exactly what every exhausted person wants to hear.

— I mean emotionally terrible, not physically.

— Somehow, that isn't better.

Clara laughed softly.

— What's wrong?

Mara leaned back in her chair and looked toward the window.

— I don't know. I think I'm just tired of making decisions.

— That's not exactly a crisis.

— It feels like one.

There was a brief silence on the other end.

— Is this about work?

— Partly.

— And the rest?

Mara hesitated.

— Everything else.

She told Clara about the promotion she had been offered, the possibility of moving to another city, and the relationship she had recently ended because neither of them seemed willing to make the sacrifices necessary to keep it alive. None of the problems were dramatic individually, but together they had become an exhausting weight that Mara carried from one day to the next.

Clara listened without interrupting.

When Mara finally finished, her sister took a deep breath.

— If you were asking me what I would do, I'd probably tell you not to make any major decisions tonight.

Mara smiled.

— That's very responsible advice.

— I'm serious. You would regret making a life-changing decision while you're exhausted and upset.

— So what would you do instead?

— I'd sleep. Then I'd write down what I actually want, without thinking about what everyone else expects from me.

Mara looked at the unfinished report on her laptop.

— And if I still don't know?

— Then I'd give myself more time.

The simplicity of the answer surprised her.

For years, Mara had treated uncertainty as something that needed to be eliminated. Every unanswered question had felt like a problem waiting to be solved. She had accepted jobs because they seemed sensible, stayed in relationships because they seemed stable, and rejected opportunities because they seemed too risky. She had mistaken predictability for happiness more times than she cared to admit.

— You know — Clara continued —, if I were in your position, I would talk to someone who knows you well before accepting the promotion.

— You mean you?

— Obviously.

Mara laughed.

— You're very modest.

— I'm also free.

They continued talking for another hour. Clara did not tell her what decision to make. Instead, she asked questions that forced Mara to examine what she actually wanted. Would she still want the promotion if it came without the impressive title? Would she move if nobody else had an opinion about it? Would she stay in the relationship if she knew she wasn't afraid of being alone?

By the time they said goodbye, Mara's problems had not disappeared.

But they no longer seemed impossible.

She closed the laptop without finishing the report.

For once, she decided that tomorrow could deal with tomorrow's problems.

The following morning, Mara woke earlier than usual. The rain had stopped, leaving the city washed and strangely peaceful. She made fresh coffee, opened a notebook, and wrote three questions at the top of the first page.

— What do I want?

— What am I afraid of?

— What would I choose if I weren't trying to please anyone?

She stared at the questions for several minutes before beginning to write.

There were no immediate answers. Some were contradictory. Others made her uncomfortable. But for the first time in months, she wasn't trying to find the perfect decision.

She was trying to find her own.

And perhaps that was what growing older really meant: not becoming certain about everything, but becoming brave enough to admit what you didn't know.

If someone had asked Mara that morning what advice she would give her younger self, she would have said the same thing Clara had told her the night before.

— You would do better if you stopped demanding that every decision feel certain before you made it.

Sometimes, you simply had to choose a direction and trust that you could change it later.
